entities.name: Hasmonean dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Hasmonean dynasty (140–37 BCE) was a Jewish priestly and royal dynasty that arose from the Maccabean Revolt against Seleucid Greek rule over Judea. The only period of Jewish political independence between 586 BCE and 1948 CE, the Hasmonean state achieved territorial expansion, Hanukkah's origin story, and the codification of Jewish religious law that shaped Judaism as it exists today.

The revolt began in 167 BCE when Mattathias and his sons, the Maccabees, refused to follow Antiochus IV Epiphanes' decrees outlawing Jewish practice and desecrating the Temple with a statue of Zeus. The recapture and rededication of the Jerusalem Temple in 165 BCE — celebrated as Hanukkah — became one of the most important events in Jewish history. Simon Maccabee secured political independence from the Seleucids in 140 BCE, beginning the formal Hasmonean state.

At its height under Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BCE), the Hasmonean kingdom controlled territory comparable to the biblical Kingdom of David, including Galilee, Samaria, Transjordan, and parts of the Mediterranean coast. The Hasmonean conversion of Idumean and Iturian peoples to Judaism created the demographic and religious context for later developments. Herod the Great (an Idumean by descent) married into the Hasmonean line before seizing power with Roman backing in 37 BCE.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Hasmonean dynasty achieved the only period of Jewish independence for 2,500 years, created Hanukkah, and shaped the Judaism that survived Roman conquest and the diaspora, making it foundational to Jewish history.
